edges.description: In patients meeting strict clinical and exclusion criteria for SREAT, systemic thyroid autoimmunity provides the autoimmune context within which steroid-responsive CNS neuroinflammation occurs.
Immune-mediated CNS inflammation produces subacute encephalopathy.
Steroid-responsive CNS neuroinflammation manifests clinically with generalized or focal seizures and status epilepticus.
CNS neuroinflammation impairs memory and executive cognitive function.
Diffuse encephalopathy and neuroinflammation manifest as confusion and clouded consciousness.
Steroid-responsive CNS neuroinflammation manifests clinically with gait ataxia and coordination deficits.
Steroid-responsive CNS neuroinflammation manifests clinically with sleep disturbance.
Steroid-responsive CNS neuroinflammation manifests clinically with speech disorder.
Steroid-responsive CNS neuroinflammation manifests clinically with abnormal movement.

edges.description: Limbic neuroinflammation in anti-NAE-positive cases causes prominent memory disturbance.
Limbic encephalitis presents with consciousness disturbance in the majority of anti-NAE-positive patients.
Limbic system inflammation drives psychiatric symptoms including psychosis and behavioral changes.
CNS neuroinflammation associated with anti-NAE autoantibodies contributes to seizure generation.

nodes.description: A subset of reported Hashimoto encephalopathy cases has anti-NH2-terminal alpha-enolase antibodies with limbic encephalitis, consciousness and memory disturbance, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, abnormal CSF or EEG, and immunotherapy responsiveness. Later reviews caution that anti-NAE lacks specificity, so this is modeled as a provisional subtype-associated mechanism.

nodes.description: Serum anti-thyroid peroxidase and/or anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are part of the SREAT case definition and reflect B-cell and plasma-cell autoimmune activity, but the antibodies are common in the general population and do not by themselves prove autoimmune CNS disease. This node is therefore modeled as a diagnostic and autoimmune-context mechanism rather than a direct neuronal injury mechanism.

nodes.description: Corticosteroids are the usual first-line therapy for suspected SREAT after a reasonable exclusion of infectious, toxic-metabolic, neoplastic, neurodegenerative, psychiatric, and better-defined autoimmune encephalitis mimics. nodes.description: True SREAT cases are thought to involve immune-mediated CNS dysfunction with altered mental status, seizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms, sometimes CSF or EEG abnormalities, and frequent response to glucocorticoids. The precise tissue-level mechanism remains unresolved; proposed processes include vasculitic or other inflammatory CNS injury.
